title: King v. Whitmer
citation: 556 F. Supp. 3d 680 (E.D. Mich. 2021); fee order, 2021 WL 5711102
lead: Michigan election litigation generated attorney sanctions based on inadequate inquiry, improper purpose, and continued proceedings, followed by a separate order fixing fees.

actors.name: Michigan voters and Republican elector nominees
Whitmer, Benson, and the Board of State Canvassers
Detroit, party organizations, and Robert Davis
Nine plaintiffs’ attorneys
actors.role: Counsel subject to the sanctions orders

proceedings: Court denied emergency relief December 7, 2020; plaintiffs later voluntarily dismissed.
August 25, 2021 order imposed attorney sanctions and education/referral requirements.
December 2 order fixed fees with a conditional stay pending appeals.
limits: This account covers the two 2021 district-court orders, not present appellate status or the merits of every election allegation. Plaintiffs were not sanctioned. Bar referrals were for investigation and possible discipline, not disbarment orders.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An election challenge seeks to change Michigan’s result
sections.cue: The plaintiffs’ own deadline passes while proceedings continue
paragraphs: Late on November 25, 2020, registered Michigan voters and Republican presidential-elector nominees sued Governor Gretchen Whitmer, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, and the Board of State Canvassers. A November 29 amended complaint alleged constitutional and Michigan Election Code violations and sought decertification, a result favoring Donald Trump, machine impoundment, and recounting. Hundreds of exhibit pages included affidavits reused from earlier challenges and purported expert analyses.

Detroit, the Democratic National Committee and Michigan Democratic Party, and voter Robert Davis intervened. On December 7 Judge Linda V. Parker denied emergency injunctive relief, identifying sovereign-immunity, laches, standing, mootness, abstention, and evidentiary obstacles. Counsel appealed and petitioned the Supreme Court, asserting that effective relief would be unavailable after the December 14 electoral vote. They nevertheless continued district-court proceedings afterward and voluntarily dismissed in January. Sanctions proceedings remained.

sections.title: Sanctions motions receive a separate hearing
sections.cue: The court identifies responsible counsel and sources of authority
paragraphs: Detroit served its Rule 11 motion December 15 and filed January 5 after the safe harbor. It also sought 28 U.S.C. § 1927 relief through its dismissal motion; the State Defendants and Davis sought sanctions as well. A July 12, 2021 hearing lasted almost six hours. Lawyers could retain counsel, answer questions, submit briefs, and provide post-hearing affidavits; none supplied the offered affidavits.

Parker considered Sidney Powell, L. Lin Wood, Emily Newman, Julia Z. Haller, Brandon Johnson, Scott Hagerstrom, Howard Kleinhendler, Gregory Rohl, and Stefanie Lynn Junttila. She did not sanction their clients because the record did not show they caused the violations.

Rule 11 required an objectively reasonable inquiry into factual support, legal warrant or nonfrivolous legal change, and proper purpose; sincere belief alone was insufficient. Section 1927 required more than inadvertence or negligence under the Sixth Circuit’s objective standard and targeted unreasonable continuation after December 14, not the initial filing alone. The injunction appeal did not divest all district-court authority, and no stay existed. Inherent-authority fees separately required meritless claims, actual or constructive knowledge, improper purpose, and compensation caused by misconduct under Goodyear.

sections.title: Responsibility cannot be avoided by labels alone
sections.cue: The City’s motion supplies the Rule 11 procedure
paragraphs: Wood denied authorizing appearance or meaningful participation. The court assessed consent to assist, public acknowledgment, awareness of sanctions, failure to object to being named, and inconsistent explanations. Newman cited limited hours and no drafting; Rohl described local counsel’s last-minute receipt of a huge complaint. The court rejected categorical exemptions for consenting named cocounsel, limited work, or local status. Post-1993 Rule 11 reached responsible later advocacy, not only the original signer, but the conclusions were specific to these records.

The lawyers challenged service, specificity, and omission of a supporting brief during safe harbor. The motion identified factual, legal, and improper-purpose grounds and incorporated Detroit’s detailed earlier opposition. The local filed-motion briefing rule did not require serving that brief too, and service used counsel’s supplied addresses. Inherent-authority grounds independently had adequate notice and opportunity to respond. Parker expressly said no court-initiated Rule 11 show-cause order had issued; Rule 11 relief rested on Detroit’s motion, not invented own-initiative compliance.

sections.title: The court compares asserted violations with the underlying material
sections.cue: The problem often lies in an unsupported inferential step
paragraphs: Parker did not equate losing with sanctionable lawyering. Besides threshold barriers, she identified failure to investigate Michigan law: multiple-ballot delivery could be lawful for family or household members; hand and drop-box delivery needed no postmark; jams and problem ballots could require rescanning after canceling an earlier count.

Factual claims also exceeded their cited support. Jessy Jacob described in-person voters who had applied for absentee ballots, not people proved to have voted twice. A dog walker’s unseen bags at a post office established no connection to ballots, a counting site, or timing violations. Melissa Carone’s vans and a later news report did not establish contents, fraudulent ballots, or candidate preference. Articia Bomer’s expressed belief that workers changed votes was labeled eyewitness evidence without asking what she saw.

Recycling affidavits did not transfer counsel’s inquiry duty, and expert reliance did not cure unsupported premises. Russell Ramsland’s turnout figures conflicted with accessible official data, included prior Minnesota-Michigan locality confusion, and underwent revisions that did not excuse the original inquiry. The sanctions issue did not require another trial proving every affiant dishonest; the gap between source and asserted proposition was often enough. Parker expressly reserved whether election fraud actually occurred.

For improper purpose and inherent bad faith, she also considered a public political narrative, positions in related Dominion defamation litigation, confirmation bias, timing, and misleading accounts of purported expert Joshua Merritt’s military-intelligence credentials. Public political speech remained distinct from professional duties governing court papers.

sections.title: The August order imposes fees, education, and referrals
sections.cue: It neither fixes the fee total nor disbars counsel
paragraphs: On August 25, Parker granted the State Defendants’ and Detroit’s sanctions motions. Davis established sanctionable conduct but received no fees or costs because his intervention contributed little and consumed resources. The nine lawyers became jointly and severally responsible for reasonable State and City defense fees and costs, with amounts to follow documentation and objections.

Each had to complete twelve hours of nonpartisan continuing legal education within six months at personal expense, at least six on pleading and six on election law. The clerk was to refer them to Michigan and their licensing jurisdictions for investigation and possible suspension or disbarment. These were referrals, not nine judicial disbarments.

sections.title: December determines recoverable amounts
sections.cue: An appeal triggers a payment stay
paragraphs: On December 2, the court awarded $21,964.75 to Whitmer and Benson and $153,285.62 to Detroit, jointly and severally against the nine attorneys. It accepted much detailed billing, necessary work by multiple lawyers, litigation-related media research, and sanctions-motion work, but reduced particular entries, including $26,077 in appellate work, public-relations time, an improper post-filing review entry, and limited quarter-hour billing.

The court distinguished Rule 11 and § 1927 deterrence from compensatory inherent-authority fees and applied lodestar reasonableness rather than automatically awarding requests. Payment was due in thirty days, but the order stayed that obligation if either sanctions decision was appealed until all appeals concluded. The combined awards explain the amount exceeding $175,000; August itself had not fixed it. This is the result of those two 2021 orders, without a claim about current appellate status.
